intro: Martin Wörner plays Rachmaninoff’s C♯ minor Prelude in a private recording made in May 2005. Three tolling notes, a rush of triplets and a return in enormous chords make a small piece sound immense.

sections.label: A · Bells, then rushing triplets
sections.mNote: A–G♯–C♯ introduces the quiet chordal answer

sections.label: B · Triplets gather force
sections.mNote: The central Agitato builds towards descending chords

sections.label: C · Bell chords return
sections.mNote: The opening comes back across four staves

sections.label: D · Quiet chords over C♯
sections.mNote: A low C♯ holds beneath the final chords

cues.title: Three notes, then quiet
cues.text: A–G♯–C♯ falls through the piano in octaves, marked fortissimo. The chords that answer are marked ppp. The three-note figure returns beneath them like a bell heard through a closed door.
cues.evidence: Bosworth (1896) and Universal Edition (1910), opening upbeat and bars 1–4; Petro Kostandy’s Mutopia engraving. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune inside the triplets
cues.text: The central Agitato keeps a melody inside its running triplets. Long notes at the top of the right hand carry the tune while shorter notes turn underneath. As the passage grows, the left hand answers and the melody climbs.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, Agitato, bars 14–34: upper melody separately stemmed above triplets, with left-hand answers. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bells come back
cues.text: The return spreads the opening over four staves, two for each hand. Rachmaninoff writes fff pesante: very loud and heavy. The quiet chordal answer from the first page now fills the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, Tempo primo, bars 45–54: four-stave notation and fff pesante. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One low note remains
cues.text: The last slow chords share a held low C♯. Above it, the hands move through a short succession of harmonies to the final C♯ minor chord. The score returns to ppp.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 55–61: held low C♯, closing chords and final ppp. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
